extras.description: Carnatic instrumental (codified ca. 14th century through Purandara Dasa's pedagogical foundation and crystallized 17th-19th century through the Tamil Nadu trinity of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri), the South Indian classical instrumental tradition treating melodic instruments as gāyaki ang — singing-style — to elaborate compositions originally written for voice. source.lineage: Tamil-language Madras (Chennai) film-song playback tradition — the Kollywood parallel canon that the catalog's hindi_filmi record explicitly scopes out — codified by Ilaiyaraaja from his 1976 debut score Annakili onward across roughly 1000 films, hand-orchestrated at a rate of about one song per session and tracked on the Madras cinema-industry scoring stages at Prasad, AVM and Gemini; the defining innovation is the fusion of Tamil village folk idiom (gaana, villuppattu, therukoothu and the nadaswaram-thavil temple-and-wedding repertoire) and Carnatic melakarta-raga melody with Western symphonic orchestration, functional harmony and genuine written counterpoint, heard on Mullum Malarum (1978), Sindhu Bhairavi (1985), Punnagai Mannan (1986), Mouna Ragam (1986) and Nayakan (1987), and carried into concert form on his own How To Name It? extras.description: Tamil filmi / Kollywood playback (Madras/Chennai, core era 1976-1992), the Tamil-language film-song playback canon of the South Indian cinema industry and the largest of the regional Indian film-music traditions that Bombay-centred Hindi filmi explicitly excludes. Defined by the same playback-singer division of labour as Hindi filmi (songs cut in studio by career playback voices, lip-synced on screen by actors) applied to a different musical substrate: Carnatic melakarta-raga melody and Tamil village folk idiom — gaana, villuppattu, therukoothu, koothu rhythm, and nadaswaram-and-thavil temple-and-wedding material — set under Western symphonic orchestration with functional harmony and real written counterpoint, a 40-to-60-piece string-and-wind orchestra sectioned across a multitrack film-scoring stage rather than tracked live-to-disc. Codified almost single-handedly by Ilaiyaraaja (1943-), who from his debut score Annakili (1976) wrote roughly 1000 film scores, notated every part himself, and worked at Prasad, AVM and Gemini studios in Madras at a pace of about one song per session: Mullum Malarum (1978), Sindhu Bhairavi (1985), Punnagai Mannan (1986), Mouna Ragam (1986), Nayakan (1987), with the parallel concert projects How To Name It? (1986) and Nothing But Wind (1988) making the Bach-and-Tyagaraja synthesis explicit. Predecessor music directors M.S. Viswanathan and K.V. Mahadevan established the Tamil playback orchestra in the 1950s-60s; the singer canon runs through S.P. Balasubrahmanyam (1946-2020, roughly 40000 songs in five languages, the defining male playback voice of the era) and S. Janaki (1938-), with P. Susheela, Malaysia Vasudevan, Vani Jairam and K.J. Yesudas. The era ends with A.R. Rahman's Roja (1992), whose sampler, sequencer and multitracked-vocal method retired the live scoring-stage orchestra. Distinguished from hindi_filmi by Tamil language, Madras rather than Bombay industrial base, Carnatic rather than Hindustani raga source, and a single-auteur rather than rotating-music-director production economy — hindi_filmi's own scope note names the Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Malayalam canons as out of its bounds, and this record fills that gap; distinguished from Carnatic classical by three-minute song form, fixed notated arrangement and absence of manodharma improvisation; distinguished from Tamil folk song by studio orchestra, professional playback voice and cinema-commercial transmission.

extras.description: A production-library idiom that hardened into a listener-facing genre once trailer houses began selling their cues as albums around 2010. It differs from film scoring proper in having no dramatic function to follow — the entire form is a single monotonic crescendo — and from symphonic metal in carrying no guitars, band, or lead vocalist.

extras.description: Piano blues is the keyboard branch of the tradition, developed where a guitar was too quiet: barrelhouses, turpentine and lumber camps, and urban rent parties. The left hand supplies bass, chords and time in a self-sufficient ostinato while the right hand imitates vocal blue notes through crushed seconds and rapid tremolo, a division of labour that makes the pianist a one-person band. It encompasses everything from Leroy Carr's soft urbane accompaniment to the hammering boogie-woogie of the rent-party players, and differs from jazz stride in staying inside blues harmony and repetition.

source.name: Ars Subtilior
source.lineage: Late-fourteenth-century Franco-Cypriot courtly polyphony of circa 1370-1420 around Avignon, Foix and the Aragonese court, written by Baude Cordier, Solage, Jacob de Senleches and Matteo da Perugia and preserved in the Chantilly and Modena codices — extreme rhythmic notation with simultaneous mensurations, syncopation across the tactus, chromatic inflection, eye-music heart- and circle-shaped scores, and three- or four-voice ballades and rondeaux for solo voices with vielle, harp and lute.

extras.description: Ars subtilior is the hyper-refined secular polyphony written for a handful of southern French, Cypriot and Aragonese courts between about 1370 and 1420, in the wake of the papal schism. It pushes Ars Nova mensural notation to its limit, layering conflicting mensurations, proportional shifts and cross-rhythms so dense that the surface sounds nearly free, and it delights in visually elaborate manuscript notation.
